q: Put the steps in order, from a protein antigen reaching a lymph node to antibody in the blood.
options: The antigen binds the B cell receptors of a matching naïve B cell
The B cell takes the antigen in and displays its peptides on MHC class II
A helper T cell recognizes the peptide and gives the B cell contact and cytokines
The B cell divides into a clone, and many daughters switch class
Daughter cells become plasma cells and memory B cells
Plasma cells release antibody that reaches the blood

q: Select every example of passive immunity.
options: Antivenom given after a snakebite
A measles vaccine
IgG crossing from a mother into her fetus
Recovering from chickenpox
IgA a baby swallows in breast milk
Anti-D injected into an Rh-negative mother

q: A healthy baby had almost no infections in her first four months, then several colds between six and nine months of age. What best explains the change?
options: Her thymus stopped making new T cells once she reached six months
IgG from her mother was broken down and left no memory cells
She began making her own IgE
Her own IgM switched irreversibly to IgD

q: A man has a fever and a rash. His blood contains IgM against a particular virus but no IgG against it. What does this suggest?
options: A current or very recent infection
An infection many years ago
Protection from a vaccine given in childhood
Antibody passed to him from his mother

q: An 18-month-old responds poorly to a vaccine made of a bacterium's capsule sugar alone, but well to one in which the sugar is attached to a protein. Why does the protein help?
options: The protein makes the sugar a larger target for IgM
Protein antigens do not need B cells at all
The protein stops the sugar from being broken down before B cells can reach it
Helper T cells that recognize the protein can help B cells that recognize the sugar

q: A B cell switches from making IgM to making IgG. What stays the same?
options: The heavy chain constant region
The number of antigen-binding sites on each released molecule
The antigen the antibody binds
Its ability to activate complement most strongly

q: Complete the sequence: IgG binds antigens on a bacterium → ____ → the phagocyte engulfs the bacterium readily.
options: The IgG molecules punch holes in the bacterium
Fc receptor proteins on a phagocyte bind the IgG stems
The bacterium displays its peptides on MHC class I
IgG enters the bacterium and blocks the enzymes it needs to divide

q: A student described how a B cell responds to a protein antigen. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The antigen binds B cell receptors in its natural folded shape
The B cell takes the antigen in and cuts it into peptides
The B cell displays the peptides on MHC class I to a cytotoxic T cell
A helper T cell gives the B cell contact and cytokines
The B cell expands and becomes plasma cells and memory cells

q: A breastfed baby is exposed to a gut virus that her mother had last year. Which antibody in the milk is best placed to protect the lining of her gut?
options: IgE
IgA
IgM
IgD

q: Why is IgM better than IgG at clumping bacteria together?
options: It binds antigens more tightly at each site
It is the only class able to leave the blood and enter tissue fluid
It carries more light chains than heavy chains
As a pentamer it has ten binding sites to link many cells

q: A hiker bitten by a rattlesnake recovers after antivenom. A year later he is bitten again. Will the first antivenom still protect him?
options: Yes, because the antivenom left memory B cells
Yes, because antivenom antibodies last for decades
No, because antivenom is broken down and leaves no memory
No, because the first dose made him permanently immune to the snake's venom

q: A bacterium survives and multiplies inside macrophages after being engulfed. Which defense is most important for clearing it?
options: IgA on mucous membranes
Th1 helper T cells releasing interferon gamma onto the macrophages
Complement punching holes in the bacterium while it circulates in the blood
Eosinophils releasing their granules

q: Why is a new influenza vaccine made every year, while one measles vaccine series protects for life?
options: Influenza's surface proteins keep changing, so old antibodies fit less well
Influenza vaccines leave no memory cells
Measles virus hides inside nerve cells, where antibodies can never reach it
The body cannot make IgG against influenza

q: Which antibody class crosses from a pregnant mother into her fetus?
options: IgM
IgA
IgE
IgG

q: A drug blocks the Fc receptor proteins on phagocytes, but antibody production is normal. A bacterium that releases a toxin infects the person. Predict each variable, compared with someone not taking the drug.

variables.name: Binding of IgG to the bacterium
Phagocytes engulfing IgG-coated bacteria
Neutralization of the toxin by antibody
Agglutination of the bacteria

q: Which cell releases large amounts of antibody and has cytoplasm packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum?
options: Memory B cell
Helper T cell
Plasma cell
Naïve B cell

q: A man stung by a wasp develops anaphylaxis. Before any treatment, predict each variable across the immune, cardiovascular, nervous and respiratory systems.

variables.name: Histamine and leukotrienes in the blood
Total peripheral resistance (TPR)
Plasma volume
Venous return
Mean arterial pressure
Heart rate
Airway diameter

q: The same man is given intramuscular epinephrine. Predict each variable over the next few minutes, compared with just before the injection.

variables.name: TPR
Leak of plasma from capillaries
Contractility of the ventricles
Airway diameter
Further mediator release from mast cells
Mean arterial pressure

q: Over years of untreated infection, HIV destroys a person's helper T cells. Predict each variable in the late stage, compared with before infection.

Cytotoxic T cell response to a new virus
Class-switched antibody made against a new protein antigen
Infections by microbes that rarely trouble healthy people
Amount of HIV in the blood

q: During the long middle stretch of the graph, the person feels well. What is happening?
options: The virus has been cleared from the blood and CD4 cells are slowly recovering
Virus stays at a steady level while the CD4 count slowly falls
The CD4 count is steady while the virus slowly disappears
Both the virus and the CD4 count are rising

fig.alt: A graph of untreated HIV infection over about ten years. The CD4 helper T cell count, per microliter of blood, starts near 1,000, dips sharply in the first weeks, partly recovers to about 750, then falls slowly for years and crosses the dashed line at 200 marked AIDS. The amount of virus in the blood spikes very high in the first weeks, falls to a lower steady level as cytotoxic T cells respond, then climbs again in the late years as the CD4 count collapses. Three phases are labeled along the top: acute infection, chronic phase with few symptoms, and AIDS. The first weeks are stretched out at the left, marked by a break in the time axis; the rest of the axis is in years.

q: In the first weeks, the virus curve spikes very high and then drops steeply. What mainly brings it down?
options: The virus runs out of CD4 cells to infect in the blood and lymph nodes
Antiretroviral drugs taken at diagnosis

The CD4 count rises above 1,000

q: Two days after clearing brush, a gardener develops an itchy, blistering rash in streaks on her forearms, where poison ivy touched her. She has had this rash before. Which type of hypersensitivity is it?
options: Type I, IgE on mast cells
Type II, antibody against skin cells
Type III, immune complexes
Type IV, delayed, T cells

q: In a person with hay fever, what happens when pollen lands on the lining of the nose?
options: Pollen cross-links IgE already bound to mast cells, which release histamine
Cytotoxic T cells kill the cells lining the nose
IgG and pollen form complexes that lodge in the kidneys
B cells meet the pollen for the first time and begin making IgM

q: Select every condition caused mainly by antibodies bound to a cell-surface antigen or receptor protein (type II).
options: An ABO-mismatched transfusion reaction
Poison ivy rash
Myasthenia gravis
Hay fever
Graves disease
Hemolytic disease of the newborn

q: A boy was stung by a bee last summer and had only a small, sore bump. This summer a single sting causes hives all over and wheezing within minutes. Why was the first sting harmless?

The first sting made IgM, which blocked the venom this time
His mast cells were still too immature last summer to release any histamine

q: Why is an antihistamine alone not enough to treat anaphylaxis?
options: It blocks only histamine and cannot raise blood pressure or open airways
It makes mast cells release even more histamine and leukotrienes into the blood
It blocks the adrenergic receptor proteins that epinephrine needs
It works only on hives in the skin of the arms

options: An oral antihistamine
A corticosteroid tablet
Intramuscular epinephrine

q: A woman with myasthenia gravis can hold her eyes open normally in the morning, but by evening her eyelids droop. What explains weakness that grows with use?

Her muscle fibers run out of ATP faster than normal after repeated contractions

It makes the thymus stop producing T cells
It binds and destroys the antibodies against acetylcholine receptor proteins at the end plate

q: Put the steps of a type I (IgE-mediated) reaction in order, from first exposure to symptoms.

The B cells switch class to IgE
IgE binds mast cells by its Fc region
On re-exposure, the allergen cross-links IgE on the mast cells
Mast cells degranulate, releasing histamine
Vessels dilate and leak, and smooth muscle contracts

q: A student described how anaphylaxis causes shock. One step is wrong. Which one?

Capillaries leak, and plasma volume falls
Venous return and cardiac output fall
MAP falls, and the tissues receive too little oxygen

Cyclic AMP rises and the smooth muscle relaxes
Airway mast cells release more histamine

q: The drawing on the right shows lupus affecting the skin, joints, pleura and pericardium. What mechanism damages so many different organs?

Antibody–nuclear antigen complexes lodging in small vessels and tissues
Cytotoxic T cells that each recognize a protein found only in one of those organs

q: A baby boy with SCID was well until 4 months of age, then had one severe infection after another. Why did the infections start then?

A CD4 count below 1,000 per microliter
Any fever lasting more than a week, with swollen lymph nodes

q: Three weeks after an untreated strep throat, a 10-year-old develops fever, painful joints and a new heart murmur from an inflamed valve. What best explains the link?

Antibodies against a strep protein also bind a similar protein on heart tissue
